objective: Connect a personally meaningful interest with a first Aura map, an adult teaching encounter and evidence of a useful next step.
explanation: The opening task establishes two connected practices: developing your own representation and helping another adult understand it. A small recognisable example gives later architecture a purpose. The map can be made with cards, a document or available software; its value comes from meaningful relationships and review, rather than the complexity of the interface.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Sam enjoys repairing bicycles. Sam selects a remembered repair with a relative, a current interest in restoring a bicycle and a future wish to teach basic maintenance. The three records connect through patience and practical learning. A peer could ask which part Sam wants to develop first. Nothing in this example establishes a working personal model or a delivered teaching service.
studio_steps: Choose one ordinary interest and decide whether to use personal, fictional or sample material. Write the audience for today's exercise before making the records, and leave unrelated personal history outside the pack.

Make past, present and future records in your own words. Give each a title and explain one connection. A builder can assign identifiers; a creative or civic learner can arrange cards or narrate the relationships.
Explain the map to an adult peer in five minutes. Invite their own starting interest and ask them to describe one connection back. Record their wording only within the agreed exercise scope.

Revise one unclear relationship and choose a manageable next question. Write when and with whose support you will return to it. Keep teacher-development time distinct from any Genesis session calendar.
teach_back: Ask the newcomer to explain Aura using their own three records, without repeating your definition. Notice which connection they understand and which requires another example. A useful teaching result includes their chosen next question.
evidence: Three titled records and a map explaining their relationships.
A brief peer account of what the introduction communicated.
One visible correction and a next encounter with a stated purpose.
transfer_test: Change the starting interest from a practical skill to a community question. Can the learner still make three meaningful records and explain their relationship without copying the bicycle example's categories?
review_questions: Which connection did the learner recognise immediately?
What did their explanation add to your map?
What support would make the next encounter worthwhile?
access: Offer spoken, written or tactile-card records and generous pauses. An imagined project is sufficient. Do not require intimate disclosure, a headset or an account to participate in the exercise.
extension: Prepare two entrances to the same map: a concise technical account of records and relationships, and a story that invites curiosity. Compare which entrance suits a particular adult audience.

objective: Build a small, recognisable life collection with meaningful links, review states, stable identities and chosen audiences.
explanation: Categories organise the collection, while links explain why its contents belong together. An identifier lets a record remain recognisable when its title or location changes. Review states describe what has happened to the account: an unchecked summary and a person-reviewed declaration should remain distinguishable. An unvisited category is an available choice, not a demand to disclose.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Lee groups twelve sample records under making, relationships and future intentions. A recipe links to a shared meal and a wish to learn food photography. Lee changes the recipe record's title but keeps its identifier. The old wording remains in the revision note, and only an agreed recipe excerpt appears in the adult teaching demonstration.
studio_steps: Choose three categories and make twelve brief records. Include title, date where known, the person's wording, relevant context and source. Use fictional material for any category you prefer not to discuss.

Add links across at least two categories. Label each relationship in ordinary language, such as learned with or useful for. Check whether another person can understand the link without seeing the entire collection.

Mark selected records unchecked, declared, explored, revised or revisited as appropriate. Change one account and retain the prior version and reason. A spreadsheet or paper revision slip can demonstrate this process.

Find one item through its title, category and a related memory. Then prepare an audience-limited teaching pack. Check the actual contents of that pack rather than assuming that a privacy label enforces access.
teach_back: Help an adult newcomer make three records using their own category names. Return the proposed wording for review and ask them to find one item through a relationship rather than its title.
evidence: A twelve-record collection with fields and cross-category links.
A revision showing stable identity, earlier wording and the reason for change.
Three retrieval routes and the exact records selected for teaching.
transfer_test: Rename a category and move one record to another view. Ask a peer to recover the same item and its history. Record any missing cue before changing the design.
review_questions: Which links carry meaning beyond a category label?
Can unchecked content be recognised easily?
What information left the private collection for teaching?
access: Use a dozen small cards, a narrated list or a familiar table. Let the learner choose category names and leave areas unvisited. Break entry and navigation into separate encounters if helpful.
extension: Compare a builder's field-based representation with a creative wall map. Identify the minimum shared identifiers and relationship descriptions needed to move between them without losing the learner's interpretation.

objective: Represent past, present and several possible best selves with their circumstances, resources and distinct meanings intact.
explanation: A remembered action, today's interpretation and a preferred future response answer different questions. Keeping them linked without merging them lets a person change their understanding while preserving context. A best self is conditional: the support available in a quiet rehearsal differs from that available during a busy public event. Several preferred responses can therefore coexist.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Alex recalls declining an invitation to perform music. Today Alex interprets the choice as needing preparation. A preferred future response might be a short performance with a trusted accompanist, while another best-self scenario involves listening and supporting someone else. Neither imagined version changes the remembered account into evidence that a performance occurred.
studio_steps: Choose an everyday event or a fictional scenario with manageable emotional weight. Make separate records for remembered action, current interpretation and preferred response. Label each perspective and its time clearly.

Describe the surroundings, expectations, inner wording, available resources and perceived options for each account. Add a second best-self condition that changes one resource, such as preparation time or support from another person.

Ask a peer or available model to summarise the relationships. Mark any confusion between desire and action, or past circumstances and present understanding. Save the original summary beside the person's correction.

Choose a small outside action or a rehearsal related to the preferred response. Record the intention before trying it, then describe what actually happened and which condition mattered. A planned rehearsal remains a plan.
teach_back: Invite an adult peer to explain why two preferred responses could both fit the same person. Reflect their interpretation back without deciding which account is the person's true identity.
evidence: Three linked perspectives with explicit time and context labels.
A summary correction separating intention, action and interpretation.
A small action or rehearsal record showing its conditions and next question.
transfer_test: Remove a resource from one best-self scenario. Ask the learner to revise the preferred response without rewriting the past or treating the changed plan as a personal failure.
review_questions: Where did present knowledge enter the remembered story?
Which resource changed the available response?
What would help distinguish two interpretations?
access: Offer third-person fiction, drawing or a brief spoken account. The learner can choose an ordinary event and decline deeper exploration. The exercise is reflection and teaching practice, not a demand for trauma disclosure.
extension: For a builder route, design separate perspective and event identifiers. For a creative route, present the same scene from two time perspectives while preserving the distinction between memory and imagined possibility.

objective: Give personally meaningful symbols, traditions and patterns of attraction or repulsion a clear, respectful place in the Aura.
explanation: A symbolic record explains an association rather than assuming that everyone shares it. Separate a learner's interpretation, a tradition's account and an observed experience. This permits spiritual, cultural, artistic and everyday vocabularies to coexist. The practical question is how an association helps the person notice, remember, express or choose, with its origin and audience visible.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Morgan associates a blue scarf with calm preparation because it was worn during enjoyable rehearsals. Another participant associates blue with energetic ocean activity. Their maps could use the same colour with different explanations. Morgan might choose a short listening practice before speaking, then describe the experience without presenting a colour association as a measured physical effect.
studio_steps: Select one symbol, colour, sound or ordinary phrase. State whether the association is personal, drawn from a named tradition or newly invented. Record the source you actually have and any limits on sharing it.

Connect the symbol with a memory, current feeling, aspiration and practical habit. Use the learner's own language. A builder can create tagged links; a creative learner can arrange images or spoken descriptions.

Choose an optional brief practice such as listening, contemplation or making an image. Set an intention and the guidance wanted. Afterwards, record the participant's account and distinguish it from any explanatory suggestion.

Explore an ordinary attraction-and-repulsion pair, such as wanting to speak while disliking a crowded setting. Identify a small action and support that respects both. Recheck whether the symbol still expresses the intended relationship.
teach_back: Introduce the meaning-map method to an adult who uses a different vocabulary. Ask what they want represented and what they would change. Teach the process without requiring adoption of your symbols or practice.
evidence: A symbolic record with authorship, context and source or personal origin.
A map separating attraction, repulsion and circumstances.
An optional practice account linked to a chosen ordinary action.
transfer_test: Present the association to someone who interprets the symbol differently. Can the record preserve both meanings and prevent the interface from silently replacing one with the other?
review_questions: Whose interpretation does this label represent?
What changed when the setting changed?
Which next action follows from the learner's meaning?
access: Everyday language is a complete route through the lesson. Offer silent observation or a written exercise instead of a practice. The learner chooses what remains private and what, if anything, is shared.
extension: Prototype a plural glossary in which one symbol has several attributed meanings. Test whether a newcomer can choose the intended context without assuming that the software has established a universal interpretation.

objective: Choose an editable avatar and interaction arrangement that feels recognisable and supports the learner's intended activities.
explanation: The avatar is a selected representation with a purpose, not a complete measurement of the person. The source offers simple two-dimensional, stylised and more detailed routes. Body real estate extends this into interaction design: consider which controls are comfortable, which areas should remain free and which tasks belong on a room display or in voice interaction.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Priya wants an avatar for rehearsing a community presentation. A simple character with chosen clothing and a seated option could be sufficient. Priya places slide selection on a handheld control rather than a wrist device, because both hands need to remain available for demonstrating an object. This is a proposed design preference, not a tested accessibility result.
studio_steps: Write the avatar's immediate purpose and choose a level of detail. Start with a sketch or an available editor. Use sample dimensions or a generic figure where personal images and measurements are unnecessary.

Demonstrate looking towards an item, moving or changing viewpoint, and selecting a record. Record what is actually possible in the chosen medium. A paper storyboard can show the intended sequence without claiming implemented interaction.

Make a body-and-environment control map. Compare handheld, voice, wrist and room-display options for one task. Note comfort, visibility, attention and areas the person prefers to leave free, then choose a provisional arrangement.

Observe one ordinary device interaction and revise the proposal around it. Label measured details, manual edits and aspirational features separately. Give the revised avatar and control map a version so a collaborator can follow the change.
teach_back: Ask an adult newcomer what they want their representation to support. Help them change one feature and explain its purpose. Check whether they can describe the three actions without needing your preferred appearance or control.
evidence: An avatar version with a stated purpose and provenance for its details.
A three-action demonstration or clearly labelled storyboard.
A comparison of control locations with the learner's reasons and revision.
transfer_test: Move the chosen activity from a desk to a shared room. Ask which controls, visibility and free-space requirements change. Revise the design before assuming that a comfortable desk arrangement transfers.
review_questions: Which detail makes the representation useful to its person?
What source supports each physical detail?
Which interaction interrupts the activity it should support?
access: A seated sketch, narrated storyboard or keyboard route is sufficient. No scan, bodily contact, headset or personal photograph is required. Let the learner identify comfort conditions rather than infer them from the avatar.
extension: Compare the same action on the body, in the room and through voice. A builder can document input events; a creative participant can rehearse the encounter and identify where attention shifts.

objective: Explain and test the relationship between a record's meaning, stable identity and visible address across Aura views.
explanation: The source proposes seven nested horn-torus shells with a twelve-row, twenty-four-column grid and internal and external addresses. A spatial address locates a view, separately from a record's identity. Follow the same item through a flat matrix, curved representation and linked record.
worked_example: Illustrative example: record M12 describes a community music rehearsal. It appears in a flat making category and at a chosen shell address, with a link to a future performance plan. Changing the colour or camera position should not create another rehearsal. A tabletop mock-up could demonstrate this relationship even when no three-dimensional interface is available.
studio_steps: Choose three sample records with stable identifiers and distinct meanings. Write their titles, contexts and sources. Assign visible positions in a small flat table, keeping the record identifier in a separate field from its position.

Map those records into a labelled shell sketch or an available spatial view. Show how an internal or external address refers back to the same record. Mark the mock-up as a representation of the proposed design.

Follow a record to its source, change one interpretation and retain the edit history. Move its visual placement afterwards. Check that the intended identifier, source and current interpretation can still be recovered.

Ask a peer to start from a record, change view, follow a relationship and return. Introduce a nearby item with a similar colour. Observe which title, source or address cue helps them recognise and repair the mismatch.
teach_back: Have an adult newcomer explain the difference between what the record means, where it appears and how it is identified. Let them use a library shelf or map analogy, then test it against the actual example.
evidence: A mapping of record identifiers to flat and spatial addresses.
One revised record whose history survives a layout change.
A peer's return journey and recovery from a deliberately nearby selection.
transfer_test: Replace the spatial display with a narrated route or ordinary list. Ask whether the learner can reach the same records and explain their relationships using stable identities rather than visual location alone.
review_questions: Which field identifies the record independently of its view?
What information survives a placement change?
Which cue helped the newcomer recover orientation?
access: Use labelled cards and a flat table instead of depth or motion. Provide written or spoken addresses and do not make colour the only cue. The conceptual mapping does not require XR equipment.
extension: A builder can draft an address-lookup table with duplicate checks. A designer can compare two highlighting treatments while asking the same newcomer to describe the underlying meaning, rather than merely recognise a colour.

objective: Build and teach a three-place memory route with source labels, visible ordered actions and a dependable way to return.
explanation: A memory palace joins recognisable places with selected records. Remembered, recreated and imagined elements need their own labels. A reusable route adds an ordered sequence that the learner can inspect before using it. Navigation, edits and external requests have different effects, so a saved path should say what each step would actually do.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Jo imagines a workshop with a doorway for a project brief, a bench for its source photograph and a shelf for the next task. A pinned notebook would open that route. After a revision, the pin should reach the intended current record. Cards can rehearse this without implying functioning software.
studio_steps: Select three distinct places and explain their associations. Label each remembered, recreated, imagined or blended. Attach one chosen record and its source to each place, avoiding a claim that reconstructed detail is verified memory.

Write the route as ordered steps with action, target, expected result and any condition. Include opening a source and changing a reflection lens. Identify whether each step navigates, edits information or would request another service.
Give the route a name and a clear starting cue, such as a doorway card or a pinned object in an available editor. Rehearse the sequence and change one step to match a revised intention.

Ask a peer to follow the route with one short cue. Then revise a target record and repeat the journey. Check the version reached, the displayed sequence and the peer's ability to return independently.
teach_back: Let an adult peer explain why each stop belongs in the route and how they would return to one record. Teach a recovery cue for losing the sequence rather than taking over navigation immediately.
evidence: A three-place map with memory, recreation or invention labels.
A named sequence distinguishing navigation, edits and proposed external actions.
A peer walkthrough and a repeat test after one target record changes.
transfer_test: Keep the underlying records but replace the imagined workshop with a familiar community venue or a spoken list. Can the learner rebuild the route while preserving its purpose and action order?
review_questions: Which details are remembered and which were created?
What effect does each saved action have?
How does the learner recover after losing the route?
access: A narrated journey or tactile sequence offers the same learning objective. Avoid motion-heavy exploration where it is unwelcome. The learner can choose an invented neutral setting instead of a personally significant place.
extension: Prepare a route preview that a human can inspect before replay. A builder can specify target identifiers and conditions; a creative learner can strengthen orientation through distinctive language, sound descriptions or place associations.

objective: Create a contextual language collection and test whether summaries and teaching translations preserve the person's intended meaning.
explanation: A useful glossary holds examples, audiences and circumstances as well as short definitions. Translation occurs whenever personal language becomes a summary, a planning brief or an introduction to another adult. Comparing these forms reveals changes in tone, missing conditions and added assumptions. Keep the original wording available so the person can review what each version communicates.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Ren calls a day spacious when it includes unhurried making and time with a friend. A model might turn spacious into having no commitments, losing the valued relationship. Ren could correct the summary and give a contrasting example: an empty afternoon that feels aimless. Those examples explain a personal usage without defining the word for everyone.
studio_steps: Choose ten meaningful words or phrases and write a context, example and intended audience for each. Include an ordinary ambiguous phrase. Leave an entry unresolved where the learner is still deciding what it means.

Select a short sample story and prepare three versions: personal summary, practical planning brief and adult introduction. Use an available model or ask peers to draft them, recording which method produced each version.

Compare every version with the original. Highlight an omitted condition, an altered tone or an invented assumption. Ask the learner to revise the wording and explain why the change matters for that particular audience.

Test one explanation through a newcomer's teach-back. If translating between languages, retain the original phrase and identify the reviewer actually available. Mark unresolved language questions instead of inventing confirmation from a fluent speaker.
teach_back: Explain one difficult term through a concrete situation, then invite an adult peer to supply a different example. Use their response to check the meaning, rather than judging whether they repeat your preferred phrase.
evidence: Ten contextual glossary entries with examples and audience notes.
Three attributed versions of one story with visible corrections.
A newcomer's explanation and the resulting glossary revision.
transfer_test: Move a phrase from a friendly creative invitation into a practical task brief. Ask what tone and context must change, and which personal meaning should remain. Compare the learner's intended and received meanings.
review_questions: What did the shortened wording leave out?
Whose interpretation entered the translation?
Which contrasting example makes the meaning clearer?
access: Offer speech, images, lyrics or written examples without requiring polished prose. Allow the learner's language and vocabulary. A translation awaiting a suitable human review can remain explicitly uncertain.
extension: A builder can specify glossary fields and version links. A creative participant can express the same relationship through a short performance or image description, then compare what each format makes easier to understand.

objective: Make a small source collection traceable, correctable and understandable enough for another person or Aura to continue the work.
explanation: A source pack distinguishes an original item, a person's account, an interpretation and a proposed action. A correction needs its own reason and date so a collaborator can understand the current account. Continuity includes readable context, stable identifiers, source relationships and audience choices. A file export alone does not demonstrate that those relationships survived.
worked_example: Illustrative example: a fictional community garden pack contains a dated photograph, a volunteer's recollection, a meeting note and a model summary. The summary wrongly places a planting activity in the previous month. The learner could correct it using the dated note, preserve the earlier wording and leave the volunteer's different recollection attributed rather than silently deleting it.
studio_steps: Gather five selected or fictional items representing memory, image, document, model explanation and observation. Label their origins and dates where known. Identify the audience for the exercise and any item excluded from sharing.

Choose one modest claim and trace it to the relevant source passage or image. Record what the source supports, your interpretation and an unanswered question. A citation should let the next reader find the actual item.

Make one correction with previous wording, revised wording, reason, author and date. Keep disagreement attributed where the evidence does not settle it. Connect the correction to the record that a future reader will encounter.

Export or copy the pack into another readable format and hand it to a peer. Check identifiers, source links, permissions and version history on return. Use the peer's unanswered questions to improve the handover.
teach_back: Give an adult newcomer the original and a summary. Ask what the source supports and what they would ask next. Help them follow the evidence trail themselves.
evidence: Five source-labelled items linked to one clearly stated claim.
A traceable correction retaining the earlier account and its reason.
A continuity checklist and peer handover questions after a format change.
transfer_test: Remove the original interface and give a second peer only the exported pack. Can they locate the current account, find its evidence and continue one defined task without receiving the entire project history?
review_questions: Which part of the claim is interpretation?
Can another person find the cited evidence?
What context was missing after export?
access: Use a small printed source pack or narrated labels if file operations are distracting. Provide readable excerpts alongside source locations. A fictional collection permits correction practice without exposing family or community records.
extension: Create a compact handover cover sheet with purpose, current version, open questions and audience. A builder can inspect structured identifiers while a civic or creative peer tests whether the human explanation is sufficient.

objective: Teach one personally meaningful Aura capability through a short adult encounter, independent practice and a revision informed by feedback.
explanation: Combine invitation, demonstration, learner action and a related attempt. Begin with the adult's interest and explain the relationship needed for their chosen action. The observer's account and learner's experience provide different evidence. Prepare a teaching pack that supports an independent return.
worked_example: Illustrative example: a newcomer wants to find notes for a community music session. The trainee could demonstrate making a source-linked record, let the newcomer create one for a chosen song and then ask them to locate a related equipment note. The observer would record where help was requested. No successful outcome is assumed before the encounter occurs.
studio_steps: Choose one capability from days one to nine and a consenting adult peer. Write their starting interest, preferred format, intended action and evidence of understanding. Prepare sample information and a fifteen-minute lesson outline.

Open with the person's question and a brief worked example. Invite them to perform the action while explaining their choices. Listen for meaning before offering the next cue, and leave room for repetition or a pause.

Present a related example with one changed condition. Ask a second peer to observe within the agreed recording scope. Compare the learner's account, the resulting artefact and the sequence of help actually offered.

Revise one confusing explanation or recovery step. Package the example, route, support options and way to resume. Invite the learner to choose whether to return, continue independently or ask another question.
teach_back: Ask the adult to explain the capability to an imagined newcomer using their own example. Notice whether their account includes the action's purpose, where to find its source and how to correct the result.
evidence: A lesson plan linked to the adult learner's chosen interest.
The learner's artefact, related-task attempt and agreed observer notes.
A revised reusable lesson with an independent return or recovery route.
transfer_test: Give the revised pack to another adult with different prior knowledge. Ask which first cue they need. Change the introduction around that need without adding the whole course as a prerequisite.
review_questions: Which explanation connected with this person's life?
Where did you answer before understanding the difficulty?
What can the learner now do without you?
access: Offer a screen, spoken demonstration, printed cards or a storyboard. Reduce the number of simultaneous tasks and let the adult choose pacing. Observation need not include audio, video or personal content.
extension: Prepare a technical version exposing fields and identifiers, and a creative or civic version using a meaningful story. Test both against the same action so changes in presentation do not hide a changed learning objective.

objective: Compare an ordinary learning task under selected conditions and use the observations to design a suitable pacing arrangement.
explanation: Test casual, normal and fast pacing with the person. Tempo, explanation density, sensory conditions and processing time can change the encounter. Keep observations beside the learner's account: quick completion alone does not establish understanding or enjoyment. Change one relevant condition where possible.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Casey learns a four-step route to a source record. One version presents all instructions together; another reveals a step, allows a pause and offers a recap. A teacher could record requests for help and ask which version preserved curiosity. Differences would be observations of this particular task, not a diagnosis or a general score of Casey's intelligence.
studio_steps: Select a short interface route, melody, diagram or practical task. State the cues, prior knowledge and resources needed. Record the setting and the learner's initial confidence without treating confidence as a prediction of performance.

Try a first version at the learner's chosen pace. Note observable events such as a completed step, a request for help or a return after interruption. Agree in advance what information the observer will retain.

Change one condition: pause length, amount of explanation, captioning or display density. Repeat a comparable task and invite the learner's account of effort, interest and support. Note any differences that prevent a clean comparison.

Make a learning-condition map and revise the earlier adult lesson. Include a practical recovery cue and a preferred rhythm for the next encounter. Revisit the preference later rather than turning today's choice into a fixed personal label.
teach_back: Ask an adult peer to explain which condition helped them learn and what evidence supports that view. Demonstrate how the same objective can retain its meaning while pauses, cues or formats change.
evidence: A task description and two explicitly stated learning conditions.
Observable interaction notes alongside the learner's own experience.
A revised lesson and a tested route back after interruption.
transfer_test: Use the preferred arrangement with another type of task. Does a rhythm that suits a diagram also suit a practical action? Record what transfers and what needs a new conversation.
review_questions: Which condition changed between the attempts?
What helped sustain curiosity as well as completion?
What alternative explanation could account for the difference?
access: Offer captions, voice, reduced visual density, assisted communication and extra processing time according to the adult's preference. Stop comparisons when they become tiring. A timing measurement is optional, not a requirement for participation.
extension: A builder can design a simple observation sheet with explicit event definitions. A creative teacher can compare spoken rhythm and visual sequencing while keeping the content and practical action as consistent as possible.

objective: Build and evaluate retrieval routes that return relevant records with their context, versions and chosen audience intact.
explanation: Finding an item and explaining its meaning are separate operations. Before testing retrieval, describe what a useful answer should include. The source distinguishes recall, model training and tool action: this lesson supplies a small retrieval evaluation, without assuming that locating a record changes a model or authorises an external action. A manual catalogue is enough to examine the relationships.
worked_example: Illustrative example: a performer plans a garden concert. A useful pack might include the latest song draft, its intended mood, audience feedback and an equipment note. Every file mentioning garden would not be relevant. A private rehearsal reflection might also be unsuitable for a public organiser.
studio_steps: Select a manageable collection and write six retrieval questions before searching. Include a direct title, a category route, a meaning-based query and a relationship across categories. Identify the records and context each answer should contain.

Try available title, category, linked-memory and model-assisted routes. If a tool is unavailable, have a peer use the catalogue. Record the route actually tested and do not describe an imagined search service as functioning.

Inspect returned items for missing context, irrelevant material and confusion between earlier and current accounts. Correct a metadata or relationship problem, then repeat the relevant question and preserve both results for comparison.

Repeat one question using a different agreed audience pack. Inspect the actual available contents. Ask a newcomer to recover a selected record and explain why it answers their question, using one alternative route if necessary.
teach_back: Invite an adult to search in their own language and explain the result. Ask what the returned record supports and what still needs interpretation. Show one way to recover when a familiar keyword is absent.
evidence: Six questions with expected relevant records written before the attempts.
Results identifying context gaps, version confusion and a tested correction.
An audience-scope comparison and a newcomer's independent return journey.
transfer_test: Ask for the same underlying information using an unfamiliar phrase and a narrower audience. Can the learner find an appropriate record without restoring excluded material or mistaking a summary for the original source?
review_questions: What made this item relevant to the question?
Which version belongs in the current answer?
What should this audience be able to retrieve?
access: Provide a small printed index, spoken search or clearly labelled cards. Use sample records when personal context is unwelcome. Let the learner compare two routes first and return to the remaining questions later.
extension: A builder can compare metadata fields and retrieval logs. A civic or creative learner can assess whether the resulting pack preserves the story and relationships needed for a useful decision or performance.

objective: Trace how selected records, a question, model output and human review participate in a developing personal Aura.
explanation: A model participates within the proposed Aura's records, interfaces, tools and continuing relationship. Distinguish context supplied during an exchange from changes to learned patterns. The source's nano LLM remains a development direction; today's comparison does not establish that capability.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Dani asks for a plan to practise music. A brief introduction might produce a generic schedule. Relevant records could add a shared instrument and limited evenings. A corrected pack could explain that one evening is reserved for a valued relationship. Comparing the proposals would reveal which supplied conditions were used, without assuming that the model permanently learned them.
studio_steps: Choose a modest question and make three versioned context packs: introduction only; introduction plus relevant records; and those records with a correction and clear task. Use fictional or chosen material with a stated teaching audience.

Compare responses from an available model, recording the question, context version and settings actually known. A role-play can illustrate the exchange when no model is available, but label that exercise separately from a software test.

Trace retrieval, prompt, response, review and saved result as separate stages. Mark whether the result is a draft, interpretation, accepted record or new question. Any proposed external action needs its own scope and event description.

Identify one omitted condition or appealing unsupported detail. Write a correction and a better example. Ask the learner whether the revised response recognises their intended meaning and record what still needs testing.
teach_back: Give an adult newcomer a pack and response. Ask them to identify information supplied, wording generated and the person's revision. Use a familiar assistant-with-a-folder analogy, then point out where it stops being an exact description.
evidence: Three named context versions linked to the same question.
Compared outputs or an explicitly labelled role-play with stage annotations.
A corrected response and the newcomer's account of the exchange.
transfer_test: Introduce a new time constraint without changing the underlying personal goal. Ask whether the learner knows where to add it, how to identify the affected response and what would count as a useful revision.
review_questions: Which supplied record changed the response usefully?
What was generated rather than retrieved?
What evidence would show a lasting model change?
access: A colour-free labelled flow, spoken walkthrough or paper exchange can show the stages. Do not require private records or a paid model service. Give the learner time to inspect the exact context pack.
extension: A builder can document input limits and version identifiers. A creative or philosophical participant can compare helpful initiative across a practical task and a reflective conversation, preserving each context rather than inventing one universal preference.

objective: Prepare an example collection with source and permission context, keeping learning examples separate from reserved evaluation material.
explanation: Begin with a desired capability, then show context, useful responses and why they fit. The dataset card records provenance, audience, gaps and revision. Preparing examples does not train a model; human review and a reserved test set can complete this exercise.
worked_example: Illustrative example: a fictional learner wants summaries of workshop planning notes to retain dates, unresolved questions and the next responsible person. Six sample exchanges could demonstrate the desired structure. Two different notes could be held back for evaluation, including one whose date is uncertain. Repeating a training example would test recall of that example rather than the intended changed-condition performance.
studio_steps: State one narrow capability and write a dataset card covering sources, audience, permission scope, example types, known gaps and corrections. Choose sample or personally reviewed material, keeping another person's contributions outside the collection unless their use is agreed.

Draft several question-context-response examples and explain why each response fits. Include different circumstances and one changed interpretation with its date. Keep source wording distinguishable from the desired response and the learner's judgement about it.

Review for duplicates, contradictory labels, missing conditions and lost meaning. Set aside a separate evaluation subset before making revisions that depend on its answers. Record the split and which material a hypothetical training process would receive.

Ask a second reviewer to inspect the collection's meaning and one reserved challenge. Resolve an ambiguity with the learner, then version the examples and correction log. If no training is performed, report readiness and open questions rather than model improvement.
teach_back: Help an adult peer prepare three examples for their own narrow purpose. Ask them to distinguish source, interpretation and desired response, then explain why one fresh question should remain outside the learning examples.
evidence: A dataset card with purpose, provenance, audience and known limitations.
Reviewed examples, a documented split and reserved evaluation questions.
A second review and correction log preserving the learner's intended meaning.
transfer_test: Use a reserved example with a changed responsibility or uncertain fact. Can a reviewer distinguish a context-sensitive response from a familiar phrase, and explain what further evidence a model comparison would require?
review_questions: What specific capability do these examples demonstrate?
Which condition would be lost in a simplified label?
Has evaluation material influenced the learning set?
access: Use a small card collection rather than code or a large dataset. Permit fictional examples and spoken review. The person can exclude sensitive material; completeness of personal disclosure is not the lesson objective.
extension: A builder can draft a portable example schema and duplicate report. A creative or civic participant can add contrasting contexts that reveal whether the desired structure preserves humour, uncertainty or responsibility accurately.

objective: Make a manageable decision inspectable through evidence, alternatives, assumptions, a small practical test and revision.
explanation: A reasoning map makes the relationship between observations and a choice available for review. It should contain plausible alternatives and the conditions each needs. A model's explanation is another proposal to inspect against sources. The learner's attraction to an option can remain part of the record alongside resources and consequences, without becoming evidence that the option will work.
worked_example: Illustrative example: a group is choosing between an outdoor music rehearsal and a smaller indoor session. The fictional brief includes limited equipment, uncertain weather and one participant's need for a quieter setting. Rather than declaring the outdoor option best because it sounds inviting, the learner could identify missing information, rehearse the setup and compare the available alternatives.
studio_steps: Write the desired result, affected people, available records, resources and constraints. Separate observations, interpretations and preferences. Choose a decision with manageable consequences so a small test can inform it without creating an unnecessary commitment.

Prepare at least three plausible approaches and state the assumptions behind each. Use a table, spoken comparison or visual map. Ask whose perspective is missing and what source or conversation would help include it.

Review a peer or model-generated recommendation against the actual brief. Identify an unsupported detail or omitted condition and request a revision. Record your provisional choice, confidence in it and the reasons for that confidence.

Test one important assumption through a rehearsal or small encounter. Compare expectation and observation, revise the decision or next question, and retain the earlier reasoning so the change is understandable to another person.
teach_back: Present the map to an adult peer and invite an alternative explanation. Summarise their view faithfully before choosing an observation that could help distinguish it from your current interpretation.
evidence: A decision brief separating observations, interpretations and preferences.
Alternative approaches with assumptions, sources and a provisional judgement.
A practical test, revised confidence and a reasoned next step.
transfer_test: Change a resource or include a newly affected person. Ask which assumption and part of the decision must be revisited. A strong answer can explain why an earlier choice was reasonable under its earlier conditions.
review_questions: Which observation most affected the choice?
What would change your current judgement?
Whose interests need another account?
access: Offer a short spoken comparison or three option cards instead of a dense table. Keep the first decision ordinary. A learner may use a fictional civic scenario rather than an unresolved personal disagreement.
extension: A builder can structure the map as linked claims and tests. A creative learner can narrate each option from an affected person's viewpoint, then return the newly noticed condition to the shared decision record.

objective: Make two creative versions of a personally or civically meaningful idea, then revise the work using an adult audience's interpretation.
explanation: Creative work gives an ambitious relationship a form someone can encounter. The brief names an audience, feeling, meaning and practical invitation. The audience's account may differ from the creator's intention; keeping both creates useful revision material. Source and permission notes remain attached to chosen excerpts and any model contributions, even when the final piece is short.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Taylor imagines a neighbourhood repair garden. One version is a spoken scene about borrowing a tool; another is a simple game choice about maintaining a shared resource. A peer might notice belonging where Taylor intended resourcefulness. That response would become a question for revision, rather than evidence that an imagined project already changed community behaviour.
studio_steps: Choose one relationship or future question from the Aura map. Write the intended audience, emotional quality and next encounter you want to invite. Select source material and decide which personal details remain outside the work.

Make a compact first version in a familiar medium: story, song, image sequence, performance or interaction storyboard. Record where a peer or model helped and which choices the learner reviewed and retained.

Make a second version that changes viewpoint, medium or tone while keeping the central relationship recognisable. Prepare an accessible description or transcript so another route into the work is available for comparison.

Let an adult peer encounter the piece before hearing the full explanation. Ask what they noticed, felt and understood. Compare that account with the brief, choose one meaningful revision and explain how it changes the invitation.
teach_back: Use the creative piece to introduce one Aura concept. Follow the adult learner's noticed detail, reveal the related record or design choice and ask them to explain the relationship through an example of their own.
evidence: A creative brief with audience, meaning, sources and permission choices.
Two distinct versions and an accessible route into the work.
Attributed audience responses and a revision linked to the intended invitation.
transfer_test: Show the piece to an adult audience with a different starting interest. Can the learner preserve the central idea while changing its entrance, rather than assuming that the first audience's interpretation is universal?
review_questions: Which relationship became perceptible through the work?
What did the audience understand differently?
Which revision serves the invitation rather than decoration?
access: A spoken scene, plain-text storyboard or described image sequence can be a complete creative work. Offer captions and readable descriptions. Sharing intimate personal material or publishing the piece is optional.
extension: Prototype one interaction with stated limits, or add a character facing a competing need. Make the future's consequences understandable while preserving the story's status as imagined possibility.

objective: Structure a chosen reflective dialogue so declarations, conditions, observations, interpretations and the person's corrections remain distinguishable.
explanation: The proposed Truth Engine is a research direction. Today's baseline describes prompt, conditions and record without establishing validated inference. Human review supplies meaning and may disagree with an interpretation. Genesis recording conditions belong to that separate programme, not automatically to this lesson.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Rowan says they want to help lead a creative group. A dialogue could explore the difference between enjoying preparation and wanting to speak publicly. Later, a fictional change of circumstances might alter the preferred role. A summary should preserve Rowan's explanation alongside the changed condition, rather than assign an untested probability to honesty or treat hesitation as evidence of deception.
studio_steps: Select an ordinary statement or fictional life category and define the exercise's audience. Record the prompt, date, relevant conditions and the learner's chosen words. Agree whether any notes are retained; no continuous recording or sensors are required.

Explore a concrete example and a preferred response under stated circumstances. Ask open questions about available resources and meaning. Return a short summary for correction before treating it as the learner's reviewed account.

Revisit the category through a later experience or clearly marked scenario. Compare wording, conditions and interpretations. If a proposed estimate is discussed, identify its question, inputs and missing validation rather than manufacturing a calibrated score.

Keep the original declaration, correction and later interpretation linked. Preserve a disagreement between the person's meaning and another interpretation as attributed accounts. Choose a next question the participant finds useful and confirm its intended audience.
teach_back: Practise a short reflective conversation with a consenting adult and return the summary. Ask what they recognise, what they change and what the summary cannot establish. Accept a meaning different from your first interpretation.
evidence: Baseline fields and an original declaration within the agreed scope.
A returned summary showing the person's correction and its reason.
A contextual comparison with attributed interpretations and a chosen next question.
transfer_test: Repeat the prompt after changing one circumstance in a fictional scenario. Can the teacher explain the changed response without deciding that one account invalidates the other or proves a hidden motive?
review_questions: What did the observation actually show?
Which meaning came from the participant's account?
What would a proposed probability still need to establish?
access: Use a neutral scenario, written reflection or pauses instead of live questioning. The participant can stop or choose another topic. This studio does not require trauma disclosure, treatment or a research inference about credibility.
extension: A builder can specify a versioned dialogue record with separate declaration and interpretation fields. A philosophical or creative participant can show how two coherent readings suggest different next questions without resolving them through an invented score.

objective: Describe contextual support preferences and compare responses that suit practical guidance, companionship or constructive challenge.
explanation: Support preferences depend on activity, urgency, relationship and current resources. A label such as enjoys direct advice can lose the conditions that make it useful. The source invites personal language and optional relational lenses. Today's scenarios turn those descriptions into reviewable examples, while the learner decides what an appropriate response means in each setting.
worked_example: Illustrative example: Kim wants step-by-step help when setting up unfamiliar music equipment, a quiet listening response while considering a song and a searching question when revising a familiar arrangement. The same person could welcome different initiative in each encounter. These sample preferences would not authorise a system to contact others, change equipment or infer an intimate emotional state.
studio_steps: Choose an ordinary relationship or activity, or use a fictional adult character. Describe relevant memory, present feeling and immediate wish in the person's vocabulary. Keep any model-suggested description separate until the person reviews it.

Create three scenarios seeking practical guidance, company while thinking and a challenge to an assumption. For each, state context, desired tone, initiative, useful questions and any tool access actually agreed for the exercise.

Compare two possible responses to each scenario. Ask the learner why one fits or fails, including where a pause would help. A builder can inspect context fields; a creative participant can try spoken rhythm or metaphor.

Discuss one support preference with a consenting adult, or rehearse the conversation. Retain only chosen insights. Change the urgency of one scenario and revise the response preference, keeping the earlier version and its circumstances.
teach_back: Offer an adult peer a scenario and several responses. Ask them to choose, explain their reason and improve the example. Avoid assuming that their preferred answer should become everyone's relationship rule.
evidence: Three contextual scenarios with explicit support and access preferences.
Response comparisons with the learner's reasons and corrections.
A changed-urgency version and a selected conversation insight or rehearsal note.
transfer_test: Keep the relationship but change available time and the learner's skill. Ask whether the original amount of initiative still fits. Explain the difference through the scenario rather than assigning a fixed personality category.
review_questions: Which condition made this response helpful?
Where would a pause support the person's choice?
What remains outside the agreed tool access?
access: Use everyday creative or practical situations and let the learner skip intimate themes. Written response cards can replace a live conversation. No account of another person's feelings should be invented or retained as confirmed fact.
extension: Create an evaluation card that includes two contrasting contexts for the same phrase, such as help me think. Test whether an adult reviewer can identify when to ask a question and when to offer a concrete next step.

objective: Test a capability in two changed situations and identify the knowledge, cues or support that enable adaptation.
explanation: Transfer tests an underlying relationship under changed conditions. Preserve an initial attempt before adding help. Distinguish repetition, supported adaptation and unresolved difficulty, recording where the method worked. This exercise cannot establish broad general intelligence or fixed learning limits.
worked_example: Illustrative example: an adult who can find a song through a memory route is asked to assemble sources for a community garden question. The familiar relationships are locating an item, checking its origin and following a link. A second challenge could require explaining that source to a new audience. An example card might help, but the resulting record should show that support was used.
studio_steps: Describe a familiar task and the relationships that make it work. Identify the starting information, sequence, check and useful result. Choose evidence that another person can inspect without needing the learner's full personal collection.

Design two related challenges that change an interface, audience, resource or problem. State what remains comparable. Ask the learner for an initial attempt and observe the point where they request help or choose another route.

Offer one selected cue or worked example at the point of need. Let the adult retry, then explain what transferred and what changed. Retain the support description beside the result rather than reporting an unsupported success.

Return to a challenge after a break or later encounter. Ask which cue helps recover the method. Revise the reusable lesson so it supports that return, and identify a further condition where the capability is still untested.
teach_back: After teaching a familiar action, give an adult peer a related task and watch their strategy. Ask them to name the relationship they reused before explaining your own preferred route or offering another example.
evidence: A familiar-task description and two explicitly changed challenge conditions.
Initial and supported attempts with the cues and observations recorded.
A later return, a revised lesson and a bounded capability description.
transfer_test: Create a fresh challenge that changes a different condition from the first two. Can the learner choose a useful strategy and identify when more help is needed, rather than merely reproduce the previous sequence?
review_questions: Which relationship survived the changed task?
What support altered the next attempt?
Where does the evidence stop supporting a capability claim?
access: Offer an agreed help signal and enough time for a first attempt without making struggle a spectacle. Use familiar formats where possible. Adaptation with chosen support is valid evidence and should be described accurately.
extension: A builder can create a challenge matrix showing changed and constant conditions. A civic or creative learner can translate the same source-checking method into a new subject while explaining what specialist knowledge is still needed.

objective: Integrate the first twenty days into a personally meaningful demonstration with traceable sources, correction, transfer, adult teaching and a usable handover.
explanation: Follow one question through a personal map, selected records, an exchange, review and a useful result. Show how the parts serve the intention, what support was needed and what another adult can continue. These records provide a baseline for later tools and simulations.
worked_example: Illustrative example: fictional records support a music-and-repair gathering. The learner could retrieve an equipment note, compare plans and correct an assumed availability. A newcomer might prepare a task card. This remains a rehearsal until people, resources and arrangements are confirmed, rather than an announced operating event.
studio_steps: Choose one life, creative or civic question and write purpose, intended result, audience, records and permissions. Identify the capabilities involved and acceptance evidence. Ask a peer to review whether the scope is manageable before building the demonstration.

Start at the map, follow relevant records and show a selected exchange leading to an artefact or next action. Explain one source and one correction. Distinguish draft, reviewed record, simulation and proposed external action throughout the route.

Introduce a changed condition and ask a newcomer to perform one element with guidance, then a related example. Record their explanation, the support used and any unresolved difficulty. Do not substitute a polished presentation for their attempt.

Package the brief, route, source trail, result, transfer evidence and revised plan for continuation. Ask a peer to perform one next step using only the handover, then add the context they actually needed.
teach_back: Have an adult newcomer explain how the result follows from the starting question and then carry out a small related action. Invite them to identify a source, a correction and a next choice in their own words.
evidence: A reviewed brief and coherent route through records, exchange and artefact.
A source check, visible correction and changed-condition teaching result.
A peer-tested continuation pack with support needs and revised next steps.
transfer_test: Change the audience, resource or intended outcome after the demonstration. Ask which records, assumptions and permissions must be reconsidered. Compare the revised route with the original rather than claiming universal capability from one successful encounter.
review_questions: What expanded capability does the evidence actually show?
Which part still depends on particular support?
Can another person continue without hidden context?
access: Offer several short encounters instead of one long presentation. A narrated portfolio, simple document or storyboard can demonstrate the relationships. Use sample records and the learner's chosen pacing; certification or clinical activity is outside this checkpoint.
extension: Identify a future function or specialist role that could improve the route. Describe its desired input and result for the tools movement, without claiming that it is implemented.
